_what_this_is: Population anchors for estimating how many channels exist that would pass
the filter. Figures are from published industry reporting, checked in
August 2026 — see `sources` below. They live in JSON rather than in code
so that when you find a better number you can replace it and watch the
Every figure has a band. Use the band, not the midpoint — the midpoint is
false precision and the band is the honest answer.
Nothing in this file was measured by this project. The measured numbers
live in data/build-report.json and are much smaller.

youtube: vidIQ, July 2026 — 61.2M channels analysed: 40.6% reached 1k subscribers, 7.9% reached 10k, 1.3% reached 100k (792,376 channels). https://vidiq.com/blog/post/youtube-subscriber-growth-statistics/
Total channels on the platform: ~113.9M — but most are dormant or empty, which is why the tiers below start at 1k rather than at the total.
Caveat: vidIQ's 61.2M is the set it tracks, not all 113.9M. High tiers are almost certainly complete (a 100k channel is tracked); the 1k tier probably undercounts.
twitch: 7.06M streamers broadcast during 2026; ~2.8M active channels in May 2026 alone.
~92,000-97,000 channels live concurrently on an average day.
1M+ streamers earn revenue monthly through Affiliate or Partner.
instagram: 5.9M creators have 10k+ followers (snapshot, 31 December 2025); ~3.3M of those actively post.
76.86% of influencer accounts sit in the 1k-10k nano tier, which puts 1k+ near 25M.
tiktok: NO RELIABLE FIGURE EXISTS, and the published ones disagree by more than an order of magnitude.

One widely repeated stat says 'over 1.5 million TikTok content creators globally' — plainly a narrow definition, since Creator Rewards alone requires 10k followers and far more than 1.5M accounts clear it.
TikTok publishes no creator census and there is no trustworthy third-party index.
The band below is therefore enormous on purpose. Treat any TikTok row in the output as a placeholder, not an estimate.

_note: The fraction expected to survive the teen-safe rules in safety/rules.json.
These are the softest assumptions in the file — the honest way to firm
them up is to measure a few thousand real channels and read the actual
rate out of build-report.json, then come back and edit these.
Twitch is much lower than the others for one specific reason: a large
share of active channels declare themselves mature, and the filter takes
that declaration at face value.
What this project could actually measure, which is a different question
from how many exist. Discovery ceilings, not population estimates.
Twitch is the outlier: /helix/streams really does enumerate everything
live, so daily runs converge on the active population rather than on a
sample of it.

youtube.why: 10,000 quota units/day; ~3 to measure a channel, 100 per discovery search

twitch.why: no quota, 800 requests/min; ~95k live at any moment, and daily runs union toward the ~2.8M channels active in a month

tiktok.why: no endpoint for any creator but the connected one, short of the academic Research API

instagram.why: business_discovery is a lookup by a username you already hold, not a search

_note: The pass rates above were reasoned about for channels that have an audience.
They do not hold at the bottom of the distribution, and pretending they do
is the single biggest error available in this file.
Scam channels, robux generators, engagement farms and abandoned spam all
live at 1-500 followers. They are cheap to create and there are millions of
them. A filter aimed at a 13-18 audience rejects a far larger share down
there than it does among channels anyone actually watches.
These multipliers scale the platform pass rate by tier. They are judgement,
not measurement — and unlike the population figures they can be settled
cheaply: measure ten thousand real channels at 1k-10k and read the true
rate out of build-report.json.
